topics.topic: Shanidar A: violence and care in one Neanderthal life
topics.story_premise: A 75,000-year-old Neanderthal from Shanidar Cave in Iraq survived a devastating facial injury that likely required care, yet also carries a perimortem shoulder wound consistent with a wooden spear—putting violence and compassion inside the same human story.
topics.hero_anchor: Shanidar A's perforated scapula and the reconstructed story of the individual
topics.tension_or_mystery: How can one skeleton preserve evidence of both prolonged care and lethal violence, and what can the bones actually prove?
topics.viewer_stakes: The answer changes how we imagine Neanderthals—and how ancient the roots of care, social bonds and interpersonal violence may be.
topics.why_now: A new peer-reviewed Scientific Reports paper was published on 2026-10-15 and Reuters reported the find the same day.
topics.market_signal: Neanderthal long-form has proven multi-million-view demand on YouTube, while Shanidar has existing documentary interest and low Arabic saturation for this exact new discovery.
topics.key_visual: Macro view of the scapula perforation beside a simple wooden-spear trajectory, contrasted with the cave burial context.

thumbnail_hypothesis.hero_subject: Shanidar A scapula with the visible perforation
thumbnail_hypothesis.visual_tension: A small ancient hole that implies a violent final event
thumbnail_hypothesis.composition: Large pale bone at left/center, dark Shanidar cave field behind it, one wooden spear silhouette aligned toward the perforation, strong negative space

topics.risk_notes: Do not identify a killer or claim motive. Distinguish confirmed trauma morphology from interpretation; keep the burial/care debate accurately qualified.

topics.story_premise: American companies believed they had hired U.S.-based remote engineers, while employer-issued laptops sat in ordinary U.S. homes and were remotely controlled as part of an alleged DPRK IT-worker scheme.
topics.hero_anchor: The physical laptop farms—racks of employer laptops inside ordinary American residences
topics.tension_or_mystery: How can a worker appear to be physically in the United States when only the company laptop is there?
topics.viewer_stakes: It turns remote hiring, identity checks and ordinary work-from-home infrastructure into a national-security and corporate-trust vulnerability.
topics.why_now: On 2026-10-13 the U.S. Justice Department announced coordinated actions affecting more than 70 companies and the seizure of about 187 laptops/KVM devices.
topics.market_signal: A current NBC News investigation on the scheme has over 700k views, with additional BBC coverage and active current community discussion.
topics.key_visual: Rows of company laptops with sticky notes in a domestic room, one foreground laptop appearing like a normal employee workstation.

thumbnail_hypothesis.hero_subject: One normal corporate laptop in front of a rack of many tagged laptops
thumbnail_hypothesis.visual_tension: The single 'employee' computer is physically surrounded by an impossible hidden workforce
thumbnail_hypothesis.composition: Foreground laptop and employee badge silhouette, background metal shelves packed with laptops, shallow depth, no hooded-hacker cliché

topics.risk_notes: Use allegation language for charged conduct. Do not generalize to North Korean people. Separate DOJ claims, convictions from prior cases and current charges.

topics.topic: Hera investigates what DART did to Dimorphos
topics.story_premise: Humanity deliberately slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid and changed its orbit; now ESA's Hera is closing in to inspect the aftermath and learn whether that one-off success can become a repeatable planetary-defense technique.
topics.hero_anchor: Dimorphos—the asteroid moonlet humanity deliberately struck—and the approaching Hera spacecraft
topics.tension_or_mystery: We know DART changed Dimorphos's orbit, but we still need close-up measurements of how the asteroid responded and what that means for repeatable deflection.
topics.viewer_stakes: The experiment is a prototype for how humanity might one day respond to a genuinely hazardous asteroid.
topics.why_now: Hera got its first glimpse of Didymos on 2026-10-07 and is performing its major October braking sequence as it approaches the binary asteroid system.
topics.market_signal: NASA's official DART impact broadcast has more than 5.6 million YouTube views, demonstrating proven native interest in the experiment; Hera provides the fresh second act.
topics.key_visual: Tiny Hera spacecraft approaching the enormous rough face of Dimorphos with the DART impact region as the mystery target.

thumbnail_hypothesis.hero_subject: Dimorphos dominating the frame with a tiny Hera spacecraft approaching
thumbnail_hypothesis.visual_tension: A human-made machine returns to inspect a world we deliberately hit
thumbnail_hypothesis.composition: Asteroid fills roughly two-thirds of frame, tiny gold spacecraft in opposite corner, impact region highlighted only by lighting/terrain contrast, no fake Earth-threat imagery

topics.risk_notes: Do not imply Didymos/Dimorphos threatens Earth. Do not state Hera has completed close-up inspection before rendezvous/arrival evidence supports it.
